items.title: Why Thailand’s water storage needs to be separated into climate and human parts
text: Water under pressure: Thailand irrigates 12% of its land (37–40% in the central plains), increasingly from groundwater, and faced the 2011 flood and the 2015–16 and 2019–20 droughts (Siebert et al., 2013).
GRACE sees total storage: since 2002, GRACE/GRACE-FO measure monthly changes in all water — soil, groundwater, rivers, reservoirs — from gravity (Tapley et al., 2004).
But GRACE cannot say why: a decline may come from dry years or from pumping; climate-driven and human-driven parts must be separated (Liu et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2025).
And GRACE is contaminated: the 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake left a gravity signal in Southeast Asia (Han et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007).
Gap: no study has separated climate and human storage change for Thailand with earthquake-corrected GRACE, or turned it into basin decisions.

items.title: Research questions
text: 1. How does terrestrial water storage vary spatially and temporally across Thailand after accounting for the 2004 earthquake signal in GRACE observations?
2. How much of Thailand’s storage change can rainfall and temperature explain, and is the unexplained part (TWSA residual) linked to human water use?
3. How can storage trends, climate reconstructions and residual evidence be integrated into a basin-scale decision-support system for water management?

items.title: Objectives
text: Main objective: to assess climate and human influences on terrestrial water storage change in Thailand using seismically corrected GRACE observations, climate reconstructions and independent indicators, and communicate the findings through a basin-scale decision-support system.

Specific objective 1: to quantify national and basin-scale spatial and temporal trends in terrestrial water storage using earthquake-screened GRACE products, seasonal Mann–Kendall tests and Sen’s slope.

Specific objective 2: to separate climate and human storage change with a conceptual and a random-forest model, evaluate them against GRACE and independent datasets, and test the residual against human indicators.

Specific objective 3: to develop a basin-scale decision-support system that integrates storage trends, climate reconstructions and residual diagnostics to compare basins and set management priorities.

items.title: Datasets and sources
text: Common grid: all five GRACE products and WaterGAP were regridded by nearest neighbour to one 0.25° grid (CSR native; GSFC and G3P 0.5°; GravIS 1°), set to anomalies relative to 2004–2009 and area-weighted to Thailand and the 22 basins. This is regridding, not downscaling: GRACE resolves ≈ 300 km.

items.title: Overall framework
National TWSA of the five GRACE products
text: Before Dec 2004: all five products agree month by month.
Oct–Dec 2004: a normal dry-season fall, seen by all five products — this is water, not the earthquake.
From Jan 2005: CSR and GSFC stay ≈ 150 mm below the others for the whole record. The December 2004 solution covers 1–31 Dec, so the 26 Dec earthquake shows up in January 2005.

Literature: GRACE detected the 2004 earthquake (Han et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007). COST-G and GFZ GravIS remove it (Dobslaw & Boergens, 2025), G3P is built from COST-G (Güntner et al., 2024), GSFC removes only the step (Han et al., 2013); CSR has no correction.
South: the same drop is 3–6 times larger in the southern peninsula, nearest the epicentre.

items.title: The December-2004 jump test
text: Test: CSR (−107 mm) and GSFC (−88 mm) drop while COST-G, GFZ and G3P (+59 to +63 mm) rise like WaterGAP (+15 mm). Their excess jumps (−122, −103 mm) lie outside the normal range of 780 normal months (−83 to +66 mm), and the drop grows towards the epicentre: it is the earthquake.
South: the drop is largest in the southern peninsula (CSR −397, GSFC −256 mm)

items.title: The drop is largest in the southern peninsula
text: Largest drop: southern peninsula CSR −397 mm, GSFC −256 mm, versus −60 to −115 mm in the other regions.
Why the south: it is closest to the epicentre (west of Sumatra); the gravity change fades with distance.
Not water: COST-G, GFZ and G3P show no drop in the same region.
Caution: this large signal must be removed before any trend is estimated.

items.title: Approach: detect, correct CSR and GSFC, then estimate trends
text: 1  Detect and test
2  Correct (CSR, GSFC)
3  Trend analysis
•  Five products vs WaterGAP (water only), zero line before Dec 2004
•  Excess jump = GRACE jump − WaterGAP jump
•  Placebo: 780 normal months → normal range −83 to +66 mm
•  Fit to GRACE − WaterGAP in every 0.25° cell:
•  sudden step + slow after-change (τ = 1 yr) + trend + seasons
•  Remove only the step and slow after-change
•  Five corrected products; Thailand, 22 basins, grid cells
•  Size: Sen slope (OLS as check)
•  Significance: seasonal Mann–Kendall; FDR for 22 basins

items.title: How the correction works (Thailand, CSR)
text: Why WaterGAP? It holds all water but cannot see earthquakes; it also keeps our correction independent of other 3 corrected products.
Why a slow part? The Earth keeps deforming 1–2 years after a M9 earthquake; a step alone over-corrects first and leaves a false decline later.

items.title: Two climate models: a physical model and a machine-learning model
text: Model A: physical (Liu et al., 2021)
Model B: random forest (Ji et al., 2025)
Why use both?
One model is not enough: TWSAresidual = GRACE − model, so any model error ends up in the ‘human’ part.
Different errors: a physical model (A) and a data-driven model (B) fail in different ways; agreement means the result is not a model artefact.
Complementary: A is interpretable and cannot overfit; B fits non-linear and delayed responses best.
A range, not a point: the two give TWSAresidual −3.5 to −4.7 (A) and −2.6 to −3.8 mm/yr (B) — a bracket of the human signal.
Same inputs: only rain and temperature, so neither can learn pumping (Liu et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2025).
How: one water store; keeps part of last month’s storage and adds rain; drainage set by rain and temperature (3 parameters, MCMC).
+ physically based, hard to overfit.
− one store, simple delays.
How: 300 decision trees use 15 rain and temperature inputs (lags, 3–36-month sums, season); output = average of all trees.
+ flexible, captures delays and droughts.
− can overfit → tested on unseen years.

items.title: Both models learn detrended GRACE TWSA; their output is TWSAclimate
tables: Model A: physical storage (Liu et al., 2021)
Model B: random forest (Ji et al., 2025)
One store: Sₜ = Sₜ₋₁ · exp(τₜ) + Pₜ,  τₜ = a + b·P′ₜ + c·T′ₜ
Average of K regression trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample of months
Monthly P (CHIRPS v2.0) and T (GHCN-CAMS), 1981–2024; P′ and T′ scaled to 0–1
15 features: P of current and 3 previous months; P summed over 3, 6, 12, 24 and 36 months; T of current and previous month; T 3- and 12-month means; sine and cosine of month
Detrended GRACE TWSA of each product (trend removed using training months only); output = TWSAclimate
a ∈ [−3, 0] (base drainage), b ∈ [−3, 0] (rainfall effect), c ∈ [−3, 1.5] (temperature effect)
K = 300 trees; at least 4 months per leaf; 50% of features tried at each split; no depth limit
Bounded least squares from 8 starting sets, then adaptive Metropolis MCMC: 4 chains × 8,000 iterations (3,000 burn-in); posterior median used
Fitted on training months; settings checked on a 108-combination grid with blocked 2-year cross-validation inside 2002–2015
1981–2001 spin-up from equilibrium; accepted when R̂ < 1.1 and effective sample size > 1,000
Test years are never used for fitting or for choosing settings
Prediction test: train 2002–2015, test 2016–2024 · Reverse test: train 2010–2024, test 2002–2009 · Metrics: r, NSE, RMSE

items.title: Why the models learn detrended GRACE TWSA (and not GRACE directly)
text: Why detrend? GRACE’s long-term decline contains human water use. Trained on raw GRACE, a flexible model (Model B) could reproduce that decline from slowly changing inputs (3-year rain sums, warming) and hide the human loss inside TWSAclimate. With the trend removed (fitted on training months only), both models learn only the climate-driven ups and downs, and the trend stays in TWSAresidual.

Why not GRACE − WaterGAP or GLDAS directly? GLDAS has no groundwater or rivers, and WaterGAP is not fitted to Thailand; their own errors would go straight into the residual. Our models match GRACE better on unseen years (see the results).

items.title: TWSAresidual and the human indicators used to test it
text: Residual: TWSAresidual = corrected GRACE TWSA − TWSAclimate = human water use + model error.
Reservoirs (b): monthly MSEA-Res storage of 27 large reservoirs (73 months).
Wells (a): GROW groundwater levels, 511 wells, annual 2013–2022.
Irrigation (a, c): groundwater share of irrigation and irrigated area (FAO GMIA v5) — concentrated in the central plains.
Basin test: if the residual is human, its agreement with wells should be higher where more irrigation water is pumped from groundwater.

items.title: How the two failing products are corrected: CSR and GSFC
text: Left (a, c): GRACE − WaterGAP drops at the earthquake; the red curve is the fitted earthquake shape — CSR step ≈ −100 mm, total ≈ −140 mm; GSFC step ≈ −94 mm, total ≈ −111 mm.
Why GSFC is smaller: GSFC already removes part of the step itself.
Right (b, d): removing only the red shape lifts both products back to the level of GFZ GravIS; floods, droughts and the trend are untouched.
Note: the slow slide after 2010 in (a, c) is real water loss — it stays in the data.
South: the removed signal is largest near the epicentre — ≈ 650 mm in the peninsula for CSR.

items.title: CSR before and after correction: Thailand and southern peninsula
text: Thailand: jump −107 → +16 mm (WaterGAP +15); corrected CSR now runs inside/near the COST-G, GFZ, G3P band.
South: the drop is ≈ −400 mm not corrected; after correction it is close to the others until ≈ 2020, then falls further (to ≈ −200 mm), so the south stays uncertain.
Maps: the removed signal (b) is largest in the south-west, nearest the epicentre; after correction (c) the false southern loss disappears and matches (d).

items.title: GSFC before and after correction: Thailand and southern peninsula
text: Thailand: jump −88 → +16 mm (WaterGAP +15); corrected GSFC follows the other products, slightly noisier than CSR.
South: the drop is ≈ −260 mm not corrected; after correction it is close to the others until ≈ 2020, then falls further (to ≈ −200 mm), so the south stays uncertain.
Maps: same south-west pattern of the removed signal; a few strong cells remain along the western peninsula, so the south stays uncertain.

items.title: Check: corrected CSR agrees with the provider-corrected products
text: Before → after: r with the provider products 0.61–0.64 → 0.87–0.91; RMSD 62–63 → 25–29 mm.
Same ups and downs: corrected CSR follows the 2011 flood, the 2015–16 and 2019–20 droughts and the recovery of COST-G, GFZ and G3P.
Remaining offset ≈ 40 mm: our correction is anchored to WaterGAP; the GFZ products jump ≈ 45 mm more than WaterGAP in Dec 2004. Both lie in the normal range.

items.title: Check: corrected GSFC agrees with the provider-corrected products
text: Agreement is weaker than for CSR: GSFC is noisier month to month and its own partial correction leaves a different pattern.
Remaining offset: as for CSR, corrected GSFC sits below the GFZ products after 2005 (WaterGAP anchor); trends after 2005 agree.

items.title: Trends of all corrected products and the ensemble: Thailand is losing water
text: Thailand: all five corrected products decline (Sen −2.3 to −3.2, OLS −3.0 to −4.5 mm/yr); ensemble Sen −2.68 mm/yr (Mann–Kendall p < 0.001), OLS −3.57 [−5.55, −1.41] → ≈ 31 km³ lost since 2002. Uncorrected CSR/GSFC (−7.3, −6.7) overstated the loss about 2.5 times.

South: not corrected CSR/GSFC give −20 / −16 mm/yr; corrected −6.1 / −3.8; GFZ products −1.2 to −2.0; ensemble −3.1 mm/yr. The correction removes most of the false southern loss, but products still differ there.

items.title: Where the water is lost: western and central plains
text: Grid: 71–82% of cells show a significant trend in the corrected products.
Where: strongest loss in the western and central plains (−3 to −8 mm/yr); the northeast (Chi, Mun) changes little.
Basins: 19 of 22 significant (FDR q < 0.05). The far south is uncertain — nearest the epicentre.

items.title: Both models reproduce detrended GRACE TWSA for every corrected product
text: Fit: for all five corrected products, both models follow the seasonal cycle, the 2011 flood and the 2015–16 and 2019–20 droughts.
Full-record NSE: Model A 0.77–0.90, Model B 0.96–0.97. Model B fits more closely, but fit on training years is optimistic — the next item tests unseen years.
GSFC: lowest Model A fit (0.77), consistent with its noisier record.
Display: seasonal cycle removed and 3-month mean so the year-to-year match is visible; NSE is computed on the full monthly series.

items.title: Evaluation: predicted TWSAclimate vs observed GRACE and vs independent models
text: Predicted: TWSAclimate from Model A or B (rain + temperature only), one model per corrected product.
(a, b) vs observed: detrended GRACE TWSA of the same product on unseen test years — NSE A 0.44–0.91, B 0.65–0.94; 19 of 20 satisfactory.
(c, d) vs independent: WaterGAP r 0.94–0.97, GLDAS r 0.81–0.88 (GLDAS lower: no groundwater or rivers).
Meaning: TWSAclimate matches GRACE on years it never saw and agrees with independent hydrological models, so it is a credible climate estimate. Model B is best.

items.title: Predicted TWSAclimate vs detrended GRACE TWSA (each product)
text: Thailand: Model B r 0.98–0.99, RMSE 22–28 mm, NSE 0.96–0.97; Model A r 0.88–0.95, RMSE 40–64 mm, NSE 0.77–0.90.
Basin r (maps, Model B): median r 0.97–0.98 for every product; lowest in the southern peninsula basins.
Meaning: both models reproduce GRACE closely; Model B best.

items.title: Predicted TWSAclimate vs WaterGAP 2.2e (independent model)
text: Thailand: r 0.94–0.97, RMSE 33–47 mm, NSE 0.77–0.89 for both models.
Basin r (maps): median r 0.87–0.93; lowest in the southern peninsula basins.
Meaning: an independent model, never fitted to GRACE, agrees well with our climate storage.

items.title: Predicted TWSAclimate vs GLDAS Noah (independent model)
text: Thailand: r ≈ 0.8–0.85, NSE 0.48–0.69 — lower than WaterGAP.
Basin r (maps): median r 0.77–0.84; lowest in the peninsula and Northeast Khong.
Why: GLDAS stores only soil, canopy and snow water — no groundwater or rivers.

items.title: Predicted TWSAclimate vs ESA CCI satellite soil moisture
text: Thailand: Model A r 0.80–0.81, Model B r 0.71–0.83.
Basin r (maps): median 0.61–0.73; weakest in Thale Sap Songkhla and the lower east peninsula.
Note: ESA CCI is a soil-moisture fraction, so RMSE and NSE in mm cannot be computed — only r.
Meaning: satellite soil moisture, never used in the models, confirms the climate signal.

items.title: TWSA = TWSAclimate + TWSAresidual: climate gives the swings, the residual the decline
text: Climate: TWSAclimate follows the 2011 flood and the 2015–16 and 2019–20 droughts; Model B tracks GRACE closely, Model A swings more (2012, 2022).
Residual: TWSAresidual is flat until ≈ 2010 and then falls steadily to ≈ −80 mm, with only partial recovery after 2022 — the part climate cannot explain.
Agreement: the five products (bands) and both models give the same picture.

items.title: Spatial view: climate trends are near zero, so the decline is in TWSAresidual
text: GRACE TWSA (a, d): declines in almost every basin, most in the western and central plains and the south (−4 to −8 mm/yr); Thailand −3.7 mm/yr.
TWSA climate (b, e):trends near zero everywhere (Thailand: Model A −0.1, Model B −0.6 mm/yr) — rain and temperature do not explain the decline.
TWSA residual (c, f):therefore has the same pattern as GRACE (Thailand: A −3.6, B −3.1 mm/yr).
South: largest values but most uncertain (nearest the 2004 earthquake).

items.title: Human vs climate contribution: northern and central basins
text: Measure: each year, human share = |TWSAresidual| ÷ (|TWSAclimate| + |TWSAresidual|); box = 5 products × 2 models, line = median.
Climate years: floods and droughts (2008, 2011, 2019) are climate-dominated in every basin.
Human rise: after ≈ 2012 the human share exceeds 0.5 in Ping, Wang, Chao Phraya and Tha Chin, peaking 2020–23.
Caution: a share, not a volume; TWSAresidual includes model error.

items.title: Contribution: other basins and the spatial pattern
text: Mae Klong: human share rises after 2012, like the central plains.
Chi and Mun (rain-fed northeast): climate stays dominant (≈ 0.40).
Maps (all 22 basins): 2003–2009 mostly climate-dominated; 2015–2024 human share > 0.5 in the central plains and the south.
Largest increase: Ping +0.25, Tha Chin +0.23, Pasak +0.21; no change in Chi, Yom and Sakae Krang.
South: high values but uncertain (earthquake, small coastal basins).

items.title: TWSAresidual declines for every product and both models
text: Trend: TWSAresidual falls for all five products: Model A −3.5 to −4.7, Model B −2.6 to −3.8 mm/yr; every 95% interval is below zero (≈ 2 km³ per year).
When: small until ≈ 2010, then a steady fall, deepest in 2020–2023 after the drought, with only partial recovery.
Meaning: climate explains the ups and downs but not the decline; what remains = human water use + model error.

items.title: TWSAresidual vs human indicators: reservoirs and wells (Thailand)
text: Reservoirs (73 months)
TWSAresidual rises and falls with reservoir storage: r = 0.30 (Model A) and 0.39 (Model B).
Wells (only 8 years)
National r: A −0.03, B 0.11. Eight yearly values are too few to test the national TWSAresidual.
What this means
Reservoirs give partial support. The stronger test is basin by basin .

items.title: Where irrigation uses more groundwater, TWSAresidual agrees better with wells
text: Across 18 basins
Ensemble Spearman ρ = 0.61 for Model A and 0.69 for Model B.
Strongest supporting region
Yom, Nan, Chao Phraya and Tha Chin have higher groundwater dependence and stronger well agreement.
A groundwater contribution
The association supports this interpretation. Shared errors and short records still limit attribution.

items.title: How each point of the start-year chart is made
Steps 2–4: which data drop, by how much, and is it the earthquake?
text: Decision: CSR and GSFC contain the earthquake signal → corrected in Step 5 (not discarded).
COST-G GravIS, GFZ GravIS and G3P were already corrected by their providers → used as provided.
tables: Five products and WaterGAP, all set to zero before the earthquake (Apr 2002–Nov 2004)
Water cannot leave all of Thailand by 100 mm in one month
CSR and GSFC drop about 100 mm in Dec 2004; COST-G, GFZ, G3P and WaterGAP do not
Dec-2004 jump of each product minus the WaterGAP jump (23 months after − 23 months before)
The same excess jump at every month 2007–2022 (no great earthquake): 780 normal cases
Outside the 1st–99th percentile (−83 to +66 mm) = not hydrology
CSR and GSFC fail (more extreme than all 780 cases); the other three pass
Jump in each grid cell against distance from the epicentre (3.3°N, 95.9°E)

items.title: Step 5: how the earthquake signal is removed from CSR and GSFC
text: r(t) = GRACE(t) − WaterGAP(t) = α + βt + Σₘ γₘMₘ(t) + s·H(t − t₀) + p·H(t − t₀)·[1 − exp(−(t − t₀)/τ)]
Corrected GRACE(t) = GRACE(t) − s·H(t − t₀) − p·H(t − t₀)·[1 − exp(−(t − t₀)/τ)]
•  Why subtract WaterGAP first? It is a water-only model: floods and droughts cancel, the earthquake stands out.
•  Fitted separately in every 0.25° grid cell, so the correction is large near the epicentre and small far away.
•  τ chosen from 0.25–5 years by the smallest error in the southern peninsula → τ = 1 year.
•  Independent of the provider (GravIS) correction, so the two can be compared.
Right: example for Thailand, CSR (s = −113 mm, p = −24 mm).

items.title: The apparent southern hotspot is sensitive to correction
text: Spatial signature
The removed signal is largest towards the southwest and weakens away from the epicentre.
National Sen trends change
CSR: −7.3 to −3.2 mm/year. GSFC: −6.7 to −3.0 mm/year.
A remaining limitation
Southern coastal basins retain larger processing uncertainty and need cautious attribution.

items.title: Nineteen of 22 basins have significant declining trends
text: Largest ensemble declines are shown. Southern estimates remain uncertain, even where a trend is significant.

items.title: Two climate models and matched validation tests
text: Model A: physical storage
A single store retains part of last month’s water and receives precipitation. Three parameters control climate-dependent drainage.
Model B: random forest
300 trees use 15 rainfall, temperature and calendar features. Training targets are detrended GRACE TWSA; the output is TWSAclimate.
Chronological tests
Train 2002–2015, test 2016–2024; reverse test: train 2010–2024, test 2002–2009. Evaluate r, NSE and RMSE.

items.title: TWSAclimate vs detrended GRACE TWSA: scores for every product
text: NSE > 0.5 is satisfactory (red: below 0.5). Model B has higher NSE and lower RMSE than Model A in all ten tests; 19 of 20 tests are satisfactory.

items.title: TWSAclimate and two global models, each compared with detrended GRACE TWSA
text: Each bar: one model vs detrended GRACE TWSA of that product, 2002–2023. A and B were fitted to these years (fit scores, not test scores).

items.title: Independent soil moisture supports climate-related variability
text: Year-to-year TWSAclimate (seasonal cycle removed) correlates with ESA CCI root-zone soil moisture at r = 0.71–0.83. This supports shared variability, not validation of every TWS compartment or its long-term trend.

items.title: TWSAresidual maps identify consistent mainland losses
text: Mainland pattern
Central plains and eastern basins generally have negative residual trends across products and models.
Map period: 2002–2023
These maps use the common earlier interval. A backup slide gives the full-record basin statistics.
Southern separation is uncertain
Model and product differences are largest near the earthquake-affected peninsula.
